profile.feeling: Warm and universal — literally “peace, wholeness”.

examples.tr: Thank you very much and goodbye!

collocations.tr: peace be upon you (the traditional greeting)
peace and blessing (a warm, slightly formal greeting)

phrases.meaning: a traditional greeting (answered עֲלֵיכֶם שָׁלוֹם); also the Friday-night song that welcomes the Sabbath

synonyms.nuance: “hi” — borrowed from Arabic, friendly and very informal

etymology.text: Related to שָׁלָה “to be quiet, tranquil” and שָׁלַו “to be at ease”. Common Northwest Semitic: Phoenician šlm (šalōm), Aramaic שְׁלָמָא (šlāmā), Ugaritic šlm. Cognate with Arabic سلام (salām).

funFacts: Arabic سَلَام (salām) is the same word: السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ ~ שָׁלוֹם עֲלֵיכֶם; Turkish selam “hi” comes from the Arabic.
The name שְׁלֹמֹה (Solomon) is built on the same root ש־ל־ם “whole, at peace”.
pitfalls: שָׁלוֹם is both hello and goodbye — only the situation tells which.
It is also the noun “peace”: שָׁלוֹם בָּעוֹלָם “peace in the world”.
subtleties: On the phone Israelis usually answer הַלּוֹ; a call or a letter may open with שָׁלוֹם.

profile.feeling: Coffee, the first light, the office door.

examples.tr: Good morning! Do you (m.) want coffee?
Now you get it? Good morning!

collocations.tr: good morning — good morning to you (the morning exchange)

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; later in the day people switch to שָׁלוֹם or צָהֳרַיִם טוֹבִים “good afternoon”.

etymology.text: From בוקר (“morning”) + טוב (“good”).

funFacts: Hebrew builds it like German Guten Morgen, but the adjective comes after the noun: “morning good”.
pitfalls: בֹּקֶר is masculine, so it is בֹּקֶר טוֹב (not *טוֹבָה).
The traditional answer is בֹּקֶר אוֹר “morning of light”; simply repeating בֹּקֶר טוֹב is fine too.
subtleties: Said ironically, בֹּקֶר טוֹב! means “you’ve finally woken up to it!” (Wiktionary: “Finally realized?”).

profile.feeling: A bright, friendly answer to the morning greeting.

senses.def: good morning (the reply to בֹּקֶר טוֹב; literally “morning of light”)

examples.text: בֹּקֶר טוֹב, שָׂרָה! בֹּקֶר אוֹר, יוֹסִי!
examples.tr: Good morning, Sarah! — Good morning, Yossi!
Good morning to you! How are you (f.)?

collocations.tr: good morning — good morning to you

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; the other answer is to repeat בֹּקֶר טוֹב.

etymology.text: Calque of Arabic صَبَاح النُّور (ṣabāḥ an-nūr, literally “morning of light”).

funFacts: An Arabic gift: صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ — صَبَاحُ النُّورِ (“morning of good — morning of light”) is the model of בֹּקֶר טוֹב — בֹּקֶר אוֹר.
pitfalls: Only as an answer: nobody opens with בֹּקֶר אוֹר.
subtleties: Literally “morning (of) light”: אוֹר is “light”.

profile.feeling: The evening greeting — a restaurant, a lecture, a guest at the door.

examples.tr: Good evening, can I book a table?

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; in the evening Israelis also simply say שָׁלוֹם or הַי.

etymology.text: From עֶרֶב (“evening”; Wiktionary: cognates include Arabic غَرْب, “west”) + טוֹב (“good”, from Proto-Semitic *ṭāb-).

funFacts: עֶרֶב “evening” is related to Arabic غَرْب (gharb, “west”) — where the sun sets; the Maghreb (المغرب) is “the West”.
pitfalls: It greets on arrival; when you leave at night, say לַיְלָה טוֹב or לְהִתְרָאוֹת.
subtleties: עֶרֶב is masculine: עֶרֶב טוֹב, never *טוֹבָה.

profile.feeling: Bedtime, quiet, the end of the day.

senses.def: good night (when leaving at night or going to bed)

examples.tr: Thanks for the evening, good night!

profile.synonymsNone: No synonym; לַיְלָה טוֹב is the only good-night formula.

etymology.text: From לַיְלָה (“night”; Wiktionary: probably an old adverbial accusative “at night” of לַיִל, from Proto-Semitic *layl-, cognate with Arabic لَيْل layl) + טוֹב (“good”).

funFacts: Arabic لَيْل (layl) and لَيْلَة (layla, also the name Layla) are the same word as לַיְלָה.
pitfalls: Only for parting at night or going to bed — not a greeting when you arrive (that is עֶרֶב טוֹב).
subtleties: לַיְלָה ends in -ָה but is masculine — so it is לַיְלָה טוֹב, not *טוֹבָה.

profile.feeling: The standard goodbye — friendly, never wrong.

synonyms.nuance: “OK, bye!” — the typical Israeli end of a phone call (יַאלְלָה is from Arabic)

etymology.text: The infinitive of the verb הִתְרָאָה “to see each other” (Wiktionary), root ר־א־ה “to see”: literally “to see one another (again)”.

funFacts: Many languages say goodbye with “seeing again”: German auf Wiedersehen, Russian до свидания, Greek εις το επανιδείν, Turkish görüşürüz, Chinese 再见 (zàijiàn, “again see”).
pitfalls: Do not confuse it with הַתְרָאָה “a warning, an alert” — the same letters התראה.
subtleties: On the phone some people joke לְהִשְׁתַּמֵּעַ “to hear each other” instead, since nobody sees anyone.

ref.note: Wiktionary has no page for נתראה; the verb הִתְרָאָה “to see each other” is checked there.

profile.feeling: A friendly promise to meet again.

senses.def: see you! (literally “we will see each other”)

synonyms.nuance: the standard goodbye (“to see each other”)

etymology.text: The first person plural future of הִתְרָאָה “to see each other” (root ר־א־ה “to see”): “we will see each other”.

funFacts: Like Turkish görüşürüz (“we’ll see each other”) it is one verb form: the prefix נִ־ marks “we will”.
pitfalls: It is a verb form and does not change for gender: everyone says נִתְרָאֶה.
subtleties: A little warmer and more personal than לְהִתְרָאוֹת: it expects a real next meeting.

override.pos: Wiktionary files this formula as a phrase; the course gives every greeting and polite formula the part of speech INTJ (one fixed expression).

profile.feeling: A polite, caring question — to a man.

senses.def: How are you? (to a man; literally “what is your well-being?”)

examples.tr: How are you today? (to a man)

collocations.tr: how are you today? (to a man)

synonyms.nuance: the casual “how’s it going?”, the same for everyone

etymology.text: מָה “what” + שְׁלוֹם־, the construct form of שָׁלוֹם “peace, well-being”, + ־ְךָ “your (m.)”: “what is your well-being?”

funFacts: Hebrew asks about your שָׁלוֹם: in Genesis 29:6 Jacob asks about Laban הֲשָׁלוֹם לוֹ? “is he well?”
pitfalls: Gender! To a man מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ (shlomkha), to a woman מַה שְּׁלוֹמֵךְ (shlomekh), to a group מַה שְּׁלוֹמְכֶם.
A short answer is expected: בְּסֵדֶר, תּוֹדָה.
subtleties: In careful pointing מַה takes a patah and the ש a dagesh (מַה שְּׁ…); in speech it is ma shlomkha.

override.pos: Wiktionary files this formula as a phrase; the course gives every greeting and polite formula the part of speech INTJ (one fixed expression).

profile.feeling: A polite, caring question — to a woman.

collocations.tr: how are you today? (to a woman)

synonyms.nuance: the casual “how’s it going?”, the same for everyone

etymology.text: מָה “what” + שְׁלוֹם־ (“well-being”) + ־ֵךְ “your (f.)”.

funFacts: The ending ־ֵךְ “your (f.)” is the one in לָךְ “to you (f.)”; Arabic has the same feminine -ki (ـكِ).
pitfalls: To a woman only; to a man say מַה שְּׁלוֹמְךָ.
subtleties: Without vowels both are written מה שלומך — only knowing whom you speak to tells you how to read it.

override.pos: Wiktionary files this formula as a phrase; the course gives every greeting and polite formula the part of speech INTJ (one fixed expression).

profile.feeling: Easy-going, friendly, Israeli.

senses.def: How’s it going? What’s up? (to anyone)

synonyms.nuance: the standard “how are you?”, which changes for gender

etymology.text: Calque of Yiddish וואָס הערט זיך (vos hert zikh, literally “what is heard?”); נִשְׁמַע is “it is heard”, from the root ש־מ־ע “to hear”.

funFacts: A Yiddish import: vos hert zikh? “what is heard?” — word for word German “was hört sich?”
pitfalls: It does not change for gender or number — the easy all-purpose greeting.
It means “how are things?”: answer בְּסֵדֶר or הַכֹּל טוֹב, not with news you heard.
subtleties: Very common on the phone and among friends; too casual for a job interview.

lexemes.note: Invariable: the same form for a man, a woman and a group.

profile.feeling: Calm and reassuring — everything is in order.

senses.def: fine, OK, all right (of how someone is: אֲנִי בְּסֵדֶר)
decent, a good sort (of a person)

examples.tr: How are you? — I’m fine, thanks.
The boy fell, but he’s OK.
Shall we meet at seven? — OK.

synonyms.nuance: “good, well” — a warmer answer than בְּסֵדֶר

etymology.text: From בְּ־ (“in”) + סֵדֶר (“order”), probably a calque of German in Ordnung (alles in Ordnung). Compare Russian в порядке (v porjadke).

funFacts: A word you already own twice: German in Ordnung and Russian в порядке are built exactly like בְּ־סֵדֶר “in order”.
סֵדֶר is also the Passover Seder — the “order” of the evening.
pitfalls: It never changes for gender or number: אֲנִי בְּסֵדֶר, הִיא בְּסֵדֶר, הֵם בְּסֵדֶר.
As an answer to “How are you?” it is neutral, like “OK”, not “great”.
subtleties: לֹא בְּסֵדֶר means “not OK” but also “not fair, wrong”: זֶה לֹא בְּסֵדֶר! “that’s not right!”

ref.note: Wiktionary has no page for the phrase; its parts קָרָא and לְ are checked there.

profile.feeling: The friendly, everyday way to say your name.

examples.text: שָׁלוֹם, קוֹרְאִים לִי יוֹסִי, אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט.
examples.tr: Hi, my name is Yossi, I’m a student.

etymology.text: קוֹרְאִים, the present plural of קָרָא “to call; to read” (Wiktionary: from Proto-Semitic *ḳaraʔ-), + לִי “to me”: an impersonal “(people) call me”.

funFacts: Greek με λένε and Russian меня зовут use the same impersonal “they call me”.
pitfalls: The question uses אֵיךְ “how”, not מָה: אֵיךְ קוֹרְאִים לְךָ? (“how do they call you?”).
קוֹרְאִים never changes: a man and a woman both say קוֹרְאִים לִי.
subtleties: The same verb קָרָא also means “to read”: קוֹרְאִים סֵפֶר “(they) read a book”.

override.pos: Wiktionary files שְׁמִי as a noun form (“my name”); the course treats the introduction formula as INTJ, like the other greetings.

profile.feeling: Formal introductions, letters, speeches.

examples.tr: My name is Sarah, and I am the new teacher.

collocations.tr: what is your name? (formal, to a man)

etymology.text: Wiktionary: the singular form of שֵׁם “name” with the first-person possessor “my”. שֵׁם is from Proto-Semitic *šim-, cognate with Arabic اسم (ism).

funFacts: Arabic اِسْمِي (ismī) “my name” is the same word with the same suffix -ī.
pitfalls: Formal: in conversation it can sound stiff — say קוֹרְאִים לִי.
The vowel changes: שֵׁם → שְׁמִי (shmi).
subtleties: Religious speakers call God הַשֵּׁם, “the Name”.

override.pos: Wiktionary files this formula as a phrase; the course gives every greeting and polite formula the part of speech INTJ (one fixed expression).

profile.feeling: A smile and a handshake.

examples.tr: Nice to meet you, I’m Sarah.
This is Yossi. — Nice to meet you!

collocations.tr: nice to meet you (literally “pleasant to get to know”)

synonyms.nuance: “pleasant to get to know (you)” — a little more explicit

etymology.text: From נָעִים “pleasant” (Wiktionary: related to נָעַם “to please”, cognate with Arabic نَعِيم “bliss”) + מְאוֹד “very”.

funFacts: The root נ־ע־ם gives the name נָעֳמִי (Naomi, “my pleasantness”) and Arabic نِعْمَة (“blessing”), which Turkish knows as nimet.
pitfalls: Literally “very pleasant” — “to meet you” is understood, not said.
The same for everyone: it does not change for gender.
subtleties: The usual answer is נָעִים מְאוֹד back, or גַּם לִי “me too”.

profile.feeling: Gratitude — said often and easily.

examples.tr: Thank you very much for the help!

etymology.text: From the root י־ד־ה; closely related to the verb הוֹדָה “to acknowledge, to thank”.

funFacts: The Bible links the name Judah (יְהוּדָה) — the source of “Jew”, German Jude, Greek Ιουδαίος — to this verb: Leah says הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת ה׳ “this time I will thank the Lord” (Genesis 29:35).
pitfalls: תּוֹדָה רַבָּה, not *תּוֹדָה הַרְבֵּה: רַבָּה is “much”, agreeing with the feminine תּוֹדָה.
subtleties: The answer is בְּבַקָּשָׁה or עַל לֹא דָּבָר.

profile.feeling: Politeness in one word — asking, answering, handing over.

examples.tr: Thank you very much! — You’re welcome, no problem.
Here is the key — here you are.

synonyms.nuance: “don’t mention it” — only as the answer to תּוֹדָה
“no need to thank” (literally “there is nothing for which”)

etymology.text: From בְּ־ (“in”) + בַּקָּשָׁה (“request”); hence literally “in request”.

funFacts: One word, three jobs — please, you’re welcome, here you are — exactly like German bitte, Russian пожалуйста and Greek παρακαλώ; Turkish and Chinese split them (lütfen / rica ederim; 请 / 不客气).
pitfalls: It does not change for gender or number.
From a seller, בְּבַקָּשָׁה often means “here you are” — or, with a rising voice, “yes? what would you like?”
subtleties: Literally “in request”: בַּקָּשָׁה is “a request”.

override.pos: Wiktionary files this formula as a phrase; the course gives every greeting and polite formula the part of speech INTJ (one fixed expression).

profile.feeling: A modest, polite answer to thanks.

senses.def: you’re welcome, don’t mention it (the answer to thanks)

examples.tr: Thank you very much! — Don’t mention it.

examples.text: עַל לֹא דָּבָר, זֶה הָיָה תַּעֲנוּג.
examples.tr: You’re welcome, it was a pleasure.

etymology.text: עַל “for, on” + לֹא “no, not” + דָּבָר “thing, word”: “for no thing”. Wiktionary has the phrase but no etymology.

funFacts: German nichts zu danken, Russian не за что and Greek τίποτα answer thanks the same way: “(it was) for nothing”.
pitfalls: Only an answer to thanks — it never means “please”.
subtleties: A little more formal and polite than בְּבַקָּשָׁה.

profile.feeling: A small apology, a polite way through the crowd.

senses.def: excuse me (to get attention or to pass)

examples.tr: Excuse me, where is the station?

synonyms.nuance: “I am sorry” — a fuller, more serious apology; it changes for gender

etymology.text: The action noun of סָלַח “to forgive, to excuse”; the interjection comes from the noun.

funFacts: One word for “sorry” and “excuse me”, like German Entschuldigung, Greek συγγνώμη and Russian извините; Chinese splits them (对不起 / 请问).
סְלִיחוֹת are the penitential prayers said before Yom Kippur.
pitfalls: It does not change for gender; the longer אֲנִי מִצְטַעֵר (m.) / מִצְטַעֶרֶת (f.) does.
To ask a stranger something, start with סְלִיחָה — it is the polite opener.
subtleties: With a rising voice, סְלִיחָה? means “pardon? say that again”.

profile.feeling: Agreement, a quick nod.

senses.def: so, thus (in fixed phrases: אַחֲרֵי כֵּן, לָכֵן)

examples.tr: Are you (f.) at home? Yes, I’m at home.

phrases.meaning: may there be many more like it (a congratulation)

etymology.text: Wiktionary records two senses: “yes” and the older “thus, so” (archaic). The old meaning survives in אַחֲרֵי כֵּן (“after so” = afterwards) and לָכֵן (“for so” = therefore); “yes” is the answer “(it is) so”.

funFacts: כֵּן יִרְבּוּ (“may they multiply so”) is a congratulation: “may there be many more like it”.
pitfalls: כֵּן (ken, yes) and כָּאן (kan, here) are easy to confuse: watch the vowel.
subtleties: Israelis often answer a yes/no question by repeating the verb: — אַתָּה רוֹצֶה? — רוֹצֶה.
A homograph is the adjective כֵּן “sincere, honest”.

lexemes.note: Same written form and sound as the negation לֹא “not” (he:lo); as an answer it stands alone, usually followed by a pause or comma.

override.meaning: Wiktionary’s interjection לֹא is glossed “No; used in responding to questions” — exactly this concept, the answer “no”; the check misses it only because it looks for the word “answer” of the course gloss “no (the answer)”.

profile.feeling: A clear refusal; Israeli directness.

examples.tr: Do you (f.) want more? No, that’s enough.

synonyms.nuance: an Aramaic-flavoured “no / not”, alive in fixed phrases: לָאו דַּוְקָא “not necessarily”

etymology.text: From Proto-Semitic *lā. Cognate with Arabic لا.

funFacts: Arabic لا also means both “no” and “not”.
pitfalls: Hebrew uses one word for “no” and “not”: לֹא, אֲנִי לֹא רוֹצֶה (No, I don’t want).
subtleties: Israeli speech is direct: a plain לֹא is not rude, though לֹא, תּוֹדָה is the polite default.
